newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS-Finland '98 budget adds twist of austerity.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Finland '98 budget adds twist of austerity.

text.p: Finland's coalition government on Friday gave a widely expected extra twist of austerity to its proposals for next year's state budget, saying current rapid growth would cushion deeper cuts.
Total spending, projected at 187 billion markka, would in real terms be three percent down on 1997, it said. Spending corresponds to about one-third of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
The government said it plans to bring the deficit down to 15.4 billion markka, some 10 percent below its own most recent projections and nearly 40 percent down on 1997.

"I'm sure nobody would have the nerve to propose that the deficit could grow," Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto told a news conference. The budget was based on GDP growth forecast at 3.5 percent next year and 4.5 percent in 1997, the ministry said.
The plan showed Finland, keen to be among the first joiners of the European single currency, would qualify this year and stay on track next year.
The finance ministry said the public sector deficit would narrow to 0.1 percent of GDP in 1998, with public debt remaining below 60 percent of GDP.
To qualify for the EU's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), a country's public sector deficit should be at most three percent of GDP this year, and gross public debt should be no more than 60 percent.
All five parties in the coalition said they were satisfied with the proposal, due for submission to the 200-seat parliament -- where government parties hold a 141 seat majority -- on September 2.
Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said the budget brought further unity to his government, in power since spring 1995.
The proposal also included projected revenues of two billion markka from privatisations, finance ministry budget chief Erkki Virtanen said.
The plan includes a slight cut in income taxes and reduced levies on wines and lower-alcohol products -- but heavier taxes on energy and fewer tax breaks in other areas.

Financial markets, driven by international concerns, largely ignored the plan, although Kirsi Hokka, chief economist at Handelsbanken's Helsinki branch, said it would strengthen confidence in Finnish fiscal policy.
The ministry said inflation would remain low, at around one percent in 1997 and at two percent in 1998.
The current account was forecast to show a healthy 21 billion markka surplus in 1998 against 19 billion this year.
Private consumption is expected to grow by four percent this year and slightly less in 1998, it said.

But unemployment -- already at about 15 percent one of the highest rates in Europe despite a government pledge to bring it down to around nine percent by 1999 -- will still be 13.5 percent in 1998, the ministry said.
"The government aims at economic stability, at halting the rise in central government indebtedness and at improved conditions to take care of employment," it said.
Fiscal austerity and low inflation were contributing to low interest rates, which in turn would support economic growth and job creation, it said.
